A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same financial-fraud simulation study. All 28 pages of v1 and 32 pages of v2, including equations, figures, tables and appendices, support comparison despite benchmark renaming and content relocation.

before.justification: V1 reports original multi-agent simulations, model-specific fraud outcomes, ablations and mitigation experiments in Sections 4–6 and the appendices.

after.justification: V2 retains these original experiments and adds quantitative collusion analysis, adaptive-adversary testing and fraud/detection case studies.

M1.justification: Appendix D.2 adds an adaptive procedural variant: surviving malicious agents receive banned accomplices' public actions as reflective feedback and update their strategies after banning events. The underlying simulator, agent scaffolding and mitigation methods are retained.

E1.justification: The fraud dataset, categories and public/private tasks remain unchanged. Appendix D.2 adds a distinct adversarial scenario in which attackers observe accomplices' bans and adapt, extending the conditions under which monitoring is evaluated.

E2.justification: Comparator membership in the retained experiments is unchanged. The added collusion analysis uses previously evaluated DeepSeek-V3 and DeepSeek-R1; no new competing model or mitigation baseline is introduced.

E3.justification: Section 5.4 adds measurements of malicious peers commenting per post and malicious agents contacting each user. Appendix D.2 introduces five iterative banning rounds, removing 20% of malicious agents per round in a 100-benign/10-malicious environment. These are additional protocols, not revisions to the retained experiments.

E4.justification: V2 substantially expands mechanism and robustness analyses: Section 5.4 quantifies public/private coordination, Appendix D.2 tests monitoring against adaptive attackers, and Appendix F examines successful versus failed fraud and correctly versus incorrectly classified users. These extend beyond v1's collusion ablation, failure taxonomy and illustrative coordination examples.

E5.justification: Appendix F.2 newly reports ten independent runs for its monitoring assessment. V1 provides no corresponding run count, so this establishes additional reporting rather than an increase in runs. Confidence intervals, variability estimates and significance tests are still absent.

E6.justification: Existing main and appendix result values are retained. Added Tables 7–8 report public co-commenting and private multi-attacker contact distributions, including 41% versus 6% for at least two private attackers with DeepSeek-R1 versus DeepSeek-V3. Appendix D.2 newly reports recall falling roughly from 90% to 75% under adaptation; Appendix F adds qualitative outcomes.

T1.justification: The formal fraud-success metrics, capability normalization and failure definitions are unchanged. The additions introduce empirical measurements and scenarios, without new formal assumptions, derivations, theorems or proofs.

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction retain the benchmark, collusive-fraud risk, explanatory factors and mitigation contributions. The shortened conclusion emphasizes warning insufficiency and agent adaptation already claimed in v1. Renaming the benchmark does not redefine its contribution.

C2.justification: V2 interprets shared commenting and victim contact as evidence of stronger collusion, qualifies monitoring reliability under adaptation, and explains failures through insufficient trust or mixed benign/malicious behavior. The original discussion and limitations are preserved in Appendix G.

D1.justification: V2 adds a project-page link, documents the banning-feedback procedure and supplies illustrative reflection traces and monitoring logs. Existing hardware, inference settings, code link and prompt collection are retained; the latter moves from Appendix F to H.

R1.justification: The reference list and related-work discussion are unchanged. The benchmark's claimed novelty and positioning relative to prior agent-safety and fraud research remain the same.

P1.justification: V2 renames the benchmark MultiAgentFinancialFraudBench/MAFF-Bench, retitles Section 4, shortens the conclusion, adds acknowledgements and moves the discussion to Appendix G. Appendix organization expands, but most existing prose is retained.

P2.justification: V2 adds two collusion tables and appendix figures illustrating adversarial reflection and successful/failed fraud trajectories. It corrects Figure 2's mismatched caption and relocates the benign-collaboration illustration from main Figure 8 to appendix Figure 4. Existing charts retain their designs and values.

improvement.justification: Section 5.4 and Appendices D.2/F modestly strengthen support for the retained claims through direct coordination measurements, adaptive-adversary testing and concrete monitoring failures. The gains are limited by coarse robustness reporting and an inconsistency in new Table 7: DeepSeek-V3's nonzero-peer bins sum to 9.29%, while its aggregate reports 9.00%. The additions nevertheless improve empirical coverage and transparency overall.
